# **How to Use This Workbook**

##### *Reading is level one. Writing is where the skill begins.*

**Print it. Writing by hand fixes things in your memory far better than listening or typing does. That is why there** are lines on these pages. Use a pen.
**Go in order. The chapters build the way the session did. What a bubble did last time, how exposed you are to this one, then the three moves. The third move is the part everybody skips, and it decides whether the rest** mattered.
**Do every exercise. Two to five minutes each. Finish them and you leave with your own exposure number,** your own buy rule and your own sell rule.
**On the numbers. Everything here came off the live session. Teaching examples from real market history, not** promises. The shape is the point, not the exact figures.

##### **The one idea that runs through everything**

**Felix refused to give out three tickers to buy on Monday, and he did it on purpose. A ticker helps you once. Then the money rotates and you are back to asking somebody what to do. The rules are the part** you keep, which is why this workbook has blank lines in it.

# **The Feeling You Have Not Connected to Your Money**

##### *AI is moving faster than anything most of us have lived through. The discomfort is real. Almost nobody links it to their portfolio.*

For some people the worry is work. For some it is privacy. For a lot of us it is quietly the money, and that is the part nobody says out loud.
**When Felix asked the live room for an honest yes, thousands came back inside a few seconds. You are not** alone in it and you are not being silly.
But almost nobody in that room could say how much of their money was already riding on AI. Not roughly. Not **at all. You cannot act on a worry you cannot measure, so most people do nothing, and doing nothing is still** a decision.

##### *Everything happening right now feels to Felix exactly like 1999.*

**From 1995 to 2000 the Nasdaq ran up five times. Picture your portfolio five times bigger in five years.** Retirement moves closer. The plans change.
**Then came the part people prefer to forget. It fell 78%.**
A schematic of the Nasdaq through the dot-com cycle. It is a drawing of the shape, not a price chart.
Ten thousand became $2,200. Fifty thousand became eleven.
**And the real damage was never the screen. People stopped retiring. They cancelled holidays and stopped** paying for their children's education, because the plan had been built on a figure that no longer existed.

##### **The technology was real. That was never the question.**

The internet did everything it promised in 1999. Thousands of people in one room, from Canada to **Malaysia, is the proof. AI is real too, and it is being adopted faster. But real and sanely priced are two different things, and you have to hold both at once to survive this.**

# **A Great Business at an Impossible Price**

##### *Being right about the technology will not protect you from overpaying for it.*

**Sun Microsystems was a real, thriving business at the 2000 peak. Not a fraud. Two years after the crash its** own chief executive said the quiet part out loud: to justify the price people paid, he would have had to hand over everything the company earned for ten years straight, pay nobody and build nothing. Then he asked his *investors, what were you thinking?*
**Cisco made the routers that ran the internet. The picks and shovels, which is exactly how people describe** Nvidia today. In March 2000 it was the most valuable company on Earth. Buy there and you were down 89%, **waiting twenty-five years to break even. That happened in December 2025. Revenues grew the entire time.**
The wait, if you bought the best businesses of that era at or near the top.
***Amazon fell 94% first, and that was a good outcome. Around 1,100 internet companies went bankrupt and*** never came back. pets.com. Nortel, once worth roughly a third of the Canadian stock market. eToys. Webvan.

##### **The lesson in one line**

**Being right about a company does not mean you should buy it at any price. One mistake like that can cost you twenty-five years. And nobody warns you, because from inside it the story feels entirely true.**

# **Price Up. Volume Fading.**

##### *The stock is still making new highs. Fewer and fewer people are buying it. So who is holding it up?*

**Volume is how many shares actually changed hands. Those little bars along the bottom are the most ignored thing on the screen, and they are where the early warning lives.**
Early in a rally they are big. That is institutional money buying, and it is why the thing runs. Then price keeps **climbing and the bars start to shrink. Fewer buyers at every new high. Wall Street has quietly stepped out** and left it to the crowd. At the top, volume comes roaring back as selling.
The shape Felix drew before he showed a single real chart. An illustration, not a price chart.
**Peloton is the textbook case. Ten thousand dollars near the start became about $65,000, then about $5,400.** Down roughly 95%. A real product and a real company, and the volume said so before the price did.
**Beyond Meat, 2019: $10,000 to $36,000 to $13,000. Same fingerprint.**
**R U L E O N E   ·   W R I T E T H I S D O W N**
**Price up, volume fading, is the crowd on borrowed time. It is not a sell order. It is a yellow light. Pay** attention now, on your terms, and tighten your risk before the market makes it urgent on its own.

# **The Green Bar That Was Really a Red Day**

##### *A bar can close green on a day the stock actually fell. Very few people know this, and it matters.*

Someone in the chat asked about this, so Felix drew it out. It is the thing that makes people misread a chart they are otherwise reading correctly.
Shares trade electronically before the open and after the close. So a stock can collapse overnight, open far **below yesterday's close, climb all through the official session, and print a fat green bar. Close to close, it was** a bad day.
Two days, drawn out. The gap happens while the exchange is shut.
**The colour tells you what happened inside one session, not what happened to your money. Watch the height of the volume, not the colour. The trap runs both ways: a big green volume bar near a top can be almost** entirely selling.

##### **If that makes your head spin, that is fine**

It is like the first time you sat in a car and could not remember which stalk was the indicator and which was the wiper. It becomes second nature quickly. Nobody ever bothered to tell you, that is all.

# **The Heartbeat**

##### *The boring part before the exciting part. This is what following the smart money actually looks like.*

A stock falls. It stops falling. Then it does nothing at all, sideways in a tight boring channel, for months and sometimes years. No headlines. Nobody talking about it.
**Felix calls that stretch the heartbeat, and it is the only thing he looks for. It means the sellers are finished.** Then one day price breaks out of the zone and volume goes from almost nothing to a wall of it. That is the big money arriving.
The two shapes Felix drew side by side. Illustrations of the pattern, not real charts.
The shape on the right is the one that costs people money. A dip and then straight up has no base underneath **it, and it tends to come back down quickly. It is not about something starting to rally. It is about what it rallied off.**

##### **This is fifty years old**

Felix did not invent this. His oldest mentor Jerry, who died shortly before the session, learned it fifty **years ago. It is what everyone gets taught who takes a job on Wall Street. It just never reaches the rest of us.**
✎ **E X E R C I S E 8   ·   D R AW O N E**

# **Industries First. Stocks Second.**

##### *Wall Street does not go looking for stocks. It goes looking for industries.*

**Retail picks a company it has heard of and hopes. Professionals find the industry first, then look for the** strongest name inside it. That is the step the crowd skips completely.
The easy way to see an industry is to pull up its index fund and read the same shape. Is it sitting in a heartbeat, and has it broken out? Felix did this live across software, consumer discretionary, on-demand, transport and gold.
**W H AT H I S S AT U R D AY A C T U A L LY L O O K S L I K E**
Felix reads where money arrived and left that week. The week of the session it was flowing into **computer manufacturing, oil field services and consumer electronics. Then he looks at about four industries, not the whole market, and inside those, at names sitting in a heartbeat. That is the entire** job.
The shape gets Felix to the shortlist. It does not excuse him from checking the business, and he looked at free cash flow before buying.

##### **A word to strike from your vocabulary**

Felix pulled up a stock down 55% and asked the room to point at where it was cheap. Halfway down? **Further? The question has no answer, because zero is cheap too, and zero is bankruptcy. Replace** *it with one that does have an answer: can I see the money flowing in?*

# **How Big Was the Volume?**

##### *A break is a break. The size of the volume behind it tells you how much to expect from it.*

**Felix put gold on screen twice, a year apart. 2025: a heartbeat, a break, four times the volume, and a large rally. 2026: same shape, same clean break in early August, but volume only about doubled.**
Felix's read was that it is a real rally, just not the same class of move. Half the fuel underneath it.

##### **Felix's words, not a law of nature**

This is what Felix sees in the data he studies, not a rule of physics. Shapes rhyme. They do not repeat on schedule. A bigger spike raises what he expects and guarantees nothing, and he sets the stop either way.
**O N E A S S E T, T W O D I F F E R E N T J O B S**
**Felix holds physical gold and never sells it. That is insurance, not a position. What he trades is the** fund, and on that he simply takes profits. Confusing the two is how people end up holding a trade for reasons that belong to a different decision.

# **Money Never Disappears. It Rotates.**

##### *When the market goes down, where does the money actually go? Somebody is on the other side of it.*

It does not vanish. When an industry gets too crowded and too expensive, the big money rotates into the **essential. Food, power, medicine. The things that do not stop.**
Retail gets taught buy and hold forever. Institutions rotate. These are the figures Felix put on screen.
**A bubble deflating does not mean everything goes down. It means the money parks somewhere less risky,** and it happens fast enough to see inside a single trading session.

##### **And cash is not the safe harbour**

**A 1971 dollar buys about seven cents' worth of goods today. Invested, it is worth around $360. Cash is not caution. It is a slow, certain loss. Even Buffett's famous cash pile is not really cash. It sits in T-** bills.

# **Three Outcomes. Never a Fourth.**

##### *Finding the winner is the easy half. Nearly everybody gives it back.*

Felix showed a position he was down on, live, while it was still open. It did not embarrass him because of the **framework underneath it. Every position is allowed to end in exactly three ways.**

##### **A big win**

It breaks out and runs. You hold while it stays above the rising line and move your stop up behind it.

##### **A small win**

It works a little, then rolls over. The stop takes you out with something. Still a good outcome.

##### **A small loss**

It fails. The stop takes you out quickly. It costs you a little and it is over. This is normal and healthy.

##### **There is never a fourth outcome.  There is never a big loss.**

**Felix asked the room for their biggest red number. Back came minus forty, minus sixty, minus seventy-five. In his view anything past twenty or thirty percent was avoidable. Not by picking better. By deciding the exit** in advance and automating it.

##### **What a big loss actually costs you**

**You sleep badly, and you keep it from your partner. But the part people miss is that the money is stuck.** Whoever rode the Nasdaq for fifteen years back to break-even did not just lose fifteen years. They missed everything else that happened in them.

# **The Stop You Set Before You Buy**

##### *The sell order goes in at the same moment as the buy. Always, and in the same sitting.*

**A stop is an order that sells if price reaches a level you choose. It goes in the moment you buy because you are calm then. Not excited, not hopeful, not staring at a red screen at nine in the morning. You make the** decision once and never make it again.
Illustration of how the stop moves as the position works.
**Where. Slightly below the moving-average line the stock is respecting. Felix used the 50-day. Each time it** takes out a previous high, move the stop up behind it.
**How wide. Match it to how much the stock actually moves. Felix's stop on the small software name sits 20%** below price, because that stock moves 20% in a day. Anything tighter knocks him out on day two and costs **him the whole move. Most people set stops far too tight. If a few percent is your limit, buy calmer stocks.**
**R U L E T W O   ·   W R I T E T H I S D O W N**
**Set the stop when you buy. Move it up behind new highs. Never move it down. Then stop watching.** Felix set his and went to the beach, not because he is unusually disciplined, but because there was nothing left to watch.
✎ **E X E R C I S E 1 4   ·   W R I T E T H E E X I T**

# **The Recovery Math**

##### *The entire argument for small losses, in one table.*

Felix ran this live with a calculator, got it wrong twice, and said so. He is not doing this in his head, and nobody needs to.
**If you are down You need this much gain to get back to where you started Gain**
**−1%** Nothing to think about. **+1%**
**−5%** Barely noticeable. A normal week. **+5%**
**−10%** Still the comfort zone. This is where a stop should have taken you out. **+11%**
**−30%** $1,000 became $700. You now need $300 back from a $700 base. **+43%**
**−50%** You have to double your money simply to be where you already were. **+100%**
**−70%** $1,000 became $300. This is the one people are quietly sitting in. **+233%**
**Read the bottom two rows again. A big loss is not a bigger version of a small one. It is a different problem,** and close to impossible to undo. The rule about small losses is not caution. It is arithmetic.

##### **You do not need to be good at percentages**

Felix is open that he is bad at them, and it has nothing to do with being a good investor. What you need is a rule that stops you ever reaching the bottom of that table.

# **The One-Page Cheat Sheet**

##### *Screenshot this. Better still, copy it out by hand one more time.*

**Idea What to remember**
**The premise** The technology being real does not mean the price is. The internet was real in 1999. Sun Microsystems and Cisco were real companies. The gap between a great business and an impossible price is the whole problem.
**The cost of overpaying**
Cisco: 25 years to break even. Microsoft: 15. Intel: 14. Amazon fell 94% first. About 1,100 internet companies never came back at all.
**You already own it** The S&P 500 is the most concentrated in over fifty years. Top five ≈ 30%. Two index funds and a bit of gold came back at 55% AI exposure.
**Know your number** You cannot manage a risk you cannot see. Felix's own is 36%. Nobody is aiming for zero.
**Skill 1: the warning** Price grinding up while volume fades means the crowd is holding it on borrowed time. A yellow light, not a sell order.
**Colours mislead** A bar can close green on a day the stock fell, because the gap happened before the open. Watch the height of the volume, not the colour.
**Skill 2: the heartbeat** A long quiet sideways stretch means the sellers are exhausted. Buy the break above it, on big volume. Rallying off a base is a different animal from just rallying.
**Size the break** The bigger the volume spike and the longer the base, the better the move tends to be. Roughly 2× is a rally. The ones people name years later showed about 10×.
**Industries first** Wall Street looks for industries, then stocks. Read the industry through its index fund. Four industries beat the whole market.
**Rotation** Money never disappears, it parks. Out of speculative and expensive, into essential and cash-generating. In 2000 utilities rose while the Nasdaq collapsed. In 2022 energy did.
**Cash is not safety** A 1971 dollar buys about 7 cents today. Invested, it is worth around $360.
**Skill 3: protect it** Set the stop when you buy, while you are calm. Move it up behind new highs, never down. Size it to how much the stock actually moves. Then stop watching.
**Three outcomes Big win, small win, small loss. Never a fourth. Down 30% needs +43% back. Down 70%** needs +233%.
**Hours of your life** Portfolio ÷ what you save per hour = hours riding on your decisions. Then ask how many hours you have spent learning to protect them.
**Tips vs skills** A tip helps once, then the money rotates and you are stuck asking again. A skill you keep, and you can teach it to your children.
